docs.title: Oracle3
docs.text:
Build prediction-market agents that discover markets, analyze opportunities, and test strategies.

Connect agents to Kalshi and Polymarket through MCP, guide their work with reusable Skills, and develop strategies with a Python execution engine.

13 MCP tools · 6 agent Skills · Kalshi & Polymarket data · Python 3.10+

Agent quickstart · MCP tool reference · Project and contributions · GitHub

docs.title: Explore the toolkit
docs.text:
Build What Oracle3 provides Market research agents Contract discovery, resolution rules, quotes, and order books Related-contract analysis Five relationship checks, shared fees, and structured basket calculations Paper-trading workflows Simulated entries and local holdings through MCP Python strategies Strategy interfaces, risk controls, and paper/live venue adapters Agent experiments Reusable Skills, observable state, and reproducible software validation

Public market reads need no exchange credentials. MCP provides data, calculations, and a local paper ledger. Real-order execution uses the separate CLI/Python engine.

docs.title: Connect your agent
docs.text:
Install the current development checkout:

git clone https://github.com/YichengYang-Ethan/oracle3-prediction-market-agent.git
cd oracle3-prediction-market-agent
python -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/python -m pip install -e .
claude mcp add oracle3 -- "$PWD/.venv/bin/oracle3-mcp"

For other MCP clients and Windows setup, follow the agent quickstart. Published-package installation is documented in the MCP reference.

Then ask your agent:

Find Kalshi and Polymarket contracts about the next Fed rate decision. Compare their outcome definitions, resolution rules, and order-book quotes. Summarize the markets with their IDs, prices, and comparison assumptions.

Prefer an offline first task? Try the worked fee-aware calculation.

docs.title: Tools, Skills, and an execution environment
docs.text:
Use individual MCP tools for structured data and calculations, or load one of the six agent Skills for a complete workflow. The Python interfaces support strategy development and engine operations; oracle3-extras hosts optional data, venue, and wallet integrations.

For agent developers, llms.txt provides a machine-readable guide to tasks, tools, and project resources.

docs.title: From U Lab research to an open-source project
docs.text:
Yicheng Yang worked with Haofei Yu on Coinjure at U Lab and co-developed the original U Lab Oracle3 codebase. He continues to extend Oracle3 with MCP integration, reusable agent workflows, and infrastructure for experimentation.

Read the project overview and contributions for the background, current capabilities, and direction for agent research.

docs.title: Trading Monitor CLI Documentation
docs.text: The Oracle3 CLI provides comprehensive monitoring capabilities for your trading activities, positions, and portfolio status.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
The monitoring CLI displays:

  • Portfolio Summary: Total portfolio value, cash positions, realized/unrealized P&L
  • Active Positions: Open positions with current prices and P&L breakdown
  • Recent Orders: Latest order history with status, prices, and commissions
  • Market Snapshot: Real-time bid/ask prices and spreads
  • Statistics: Trading session stats including success rate and position count

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
After installing dependencies:

poetry install

The CLI is available via the oracle3 command.

docs.title: Monitor Command
docs.text: oracle3 monitor [OPTIONS]

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• --watch, -w: Enable live monitoring mode with continuous updates
  • --refresh FLOAT, -r FLOAT: Refresh rate in seconds for watch mode (default: 2.0)
  • --config PATH, -c PATH: Path to trading engine config file (optional)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Single snapshot:

oracle3 monitor

Live monitoring mode:

oracle3 monitor --watch

Live mode with custom refresh rate:

oracle3 monitor -w -r 1.0  # Update every 1 second

docs.title: Method 1: Using MonitoredTradingEngine Wrapper
docs.text:
The simplest way to add monitoring to your trading workflow:

from oracle3.core.trading_engine import TradingEngine
from oracle3.cli.utils import add_monitoring_to_engine

# Create your trading engine
engine = TradingEngine(
    data_source=data_source,
    strategy=strategy,
    trader=trader
)

# Add monitoring
monitored_engine = add_monitoring_to_engine(
    engine,
    watch=True,        # Enable live monitoring
    refresh_rate=2.0   # Update every 2 seconds
)

# Start trading with live monitoring
await monitored_engine.start()

docs.title: Method 2: Manual Integration
docs.text:
For more control, use the TradingMonitor class directly:

from oracle3.cli.monitor import TradingMonitor

# After initializing your trader and position manager
monitor = TradingMonitor(
    trader=trader,
    position_manager=position_manager
)

# Display a single snapshot
monitor.display_snapshot()

# Or run in live mode
monitor.display_live(refresh_rate=2.0)

docs.title: Method 3: Background Monitoring
docs.text:
Run the monitor in a separate thread while your trading engine runs:

import asyncio
import threading
from oracle3.cli.monitor import TradingMonitor

def run_monitor(trader, position_manager, refresh_rate=2.0):
    monitor = TradingMonitor(trader, position_manager)
    monitor.display_live(refresh_rate=refresh_rate)

# Start monitor in background thread
monitor_thread = threading.Thread(
    target=run_monitor,
    args=(trader, position_manager),
    daemon=True
)
monitor_thread.start()

# Run trading engine
await trading_engine.start()

docs.title: Portfolio Summary
docs.text:
Shows overall portfolio health:

  • Total portfolio value across all collaterals
  • Cash positions (e.g., USDC balance)
  • Realized P&L (closed positions)
  • Unrealized P&L (open positions)
  • Total P&L (sum of realized + unrealized)

Values are color-coded:

  • Green: Positive P&L
  • Red: Negative P&L
  • White: Neutral

docs.title: Active Positions
docs.text:
Displays all open (non-cash) positions:

  • Ticker symbol
  • Quantity held
  • Average cost basis
  • Current market price (best bid)
  • Unrealized P&L
  • Realized P&L (from partial closes)

docs.title: Recent Orders
docs.text:
Shows the last 10 orders with:

  • Status (FILLED, PARTIALLY_FILLED, REJECTED, etc.)
  • Side (BUY/SELL)
  • Ticker symbol
  • Limit price
  • Filled quantity
  • Average fill price
  • Total commission

Status color coding:

  • Green: FILLED
  • Yellow: PARTIALLY_FILLED
  • Red: REJECTED
  • Dim: CANCELLED

docs.title: Market Snapshot
docs.text:
Real-time market data for active positions:

  • Best bid price
  • Best ask price
  • Spread (ask - bid)
  • Spread percentage

docs.title: Statistics
docs.text:
Session statistics:

  • Runtime (how long the session has been active)
  • Total orders placed
  • Number of filled orders
  • Number of rejected orders
  • Success rate (filled / total)
  • Active positions count

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• The monitor reads state from the trader and position manager without modifying it
  • Watch mode uses Rich's Live display for efficient terminal updates
  • Recommended refresh rates:
  • High-frequency trading: 0.5-1.0 seconds
  • Normal trading: 2.0-5.0 seconds
  • Low-frequency trading: 5.0-10.0 seconds
  • The monitor runs in a separate thread/process and won't block trading execution

docs.title: Monitor shows "No positions" but I have trades
docs.text: The monitor reads from the PositionManager. Ensure your trades are being properly processed through position_manager.apply_trade().

docs.title: Live mode not updating
docs.text:
Check that:

  1. The trading engine is running and processing events
  2. The trader and position manager are being updated
  3. Your terminal supports Rich's live display features

docs.title: Performance issues in watch mode
docs.text: Try increasing the refresh rate (e.g., -r 5.0 for 5 second updates) to reduce CPU usage.

docs.title: Custom Monitoring Periods
docs.text:
To monitor specific trading sessions:

from datetime import datetime

# Record start time
monitor.start_time = datetime.now()

# Run your trading session
await trading_engine.start()

# Display final snapshot
monitor.display_snapshot()

docs.title: Monitoring Multiple Engines
docs.text:
You can create separate monitors for different trading strategies:

monitor_strategy_a = TradingMonitor(trader_a, position_manager_a)
monitor_strategy_b = TradingMonitor(trader_b, position_manager_b)

# Display side by side or sequentially
monitor_strategy_a.display_snapshot()
monitor_strategy_b.display_snapshot()

# Your existing code

# Add monitoring (one line!)

from oracle3.cli.monitor import TradingMonitor

# After initializing trader

# Show snapshot

docs.title: Pattern C: Background Monitor
docs.text:
import threading
from oracle3.cli.monitor import TradingMonitor

def run_bg_monitor(trader, pm):
    monitor = TradingMonitor(trader, pm)
    monitor.display_live(2.0)

# Start monitor thread
threading.Thread(
    target=run_bg_monitor,
    args=(trader, position_manager),
    daemon=True
).start()

# Run trading engine
await engine.start()

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
1. Start with the demo to understand what monitoring shows
  2. Use watch mode during development for immediate feedback
  3. Adjust refresh rate based on trading frequency:
  4. High frequency: 0.5-1.0s
  5. Normal: 2.0-3.0s
  6. Low frequency: 5.0-10.0s
  7. Snapshot mode is great for end-of-session reports
  8. Background threads let you monitor without blocking your code

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Q: Monitor shows no data

  • Ensure trader and position_manager are properly initialized
  • Check that trades are being applied: position_manager.apply_trade(trade)

Q: Live mode not updating

  • Verify trading engine is running and processing events
  • Check terminal supports Rich library (most modern terminals do)

Q: Performance issues

  • Increase refresh rate: -r 5.0 or higher
  • Reduce terminal window size
  • Use snapshot mode instead of live

docs.title: JSON Snapshots
docs.text:
The dashboard command can write periodic JSON state snapshots for external monitoring:

# Write state snapshots every 5 seconds
oracle3 dashboard --snapshot-json snapshot.json

# Custom interval (2 seconds)
oracle3 dashboard --snapshot-json snapshot.json --snapshot-interval 2

# Watch the snapshot file live
watch -n 1 jq . snapshot.json

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Oracle3 is an autonomous on-chain trading agent for prediction markets. It reads on-chain data, generates trade signals via AI and quantitative strategies, signs Solana transactions, and manages risk end-to-end.

docs.title: Execution Flow
docs.text:
1. Data Sources fetch live market data + news + on-chain signals
          ↓
2. AI Agent / Quant Strategy analyzes events (multi-agent pipeline)
          ↓
3. Strategy generates trade signals with confidence scores
          ↓
4. On-Chain Risk Manager validates against portfolio limits + simulates tx
          ↓
5. Trader signs tx, optionally via Jito Bundle for MEV protection
          ↓  May use Flash Loan or Atomic Multi-Leg execution
6. On-Chain Logger writes trade to Solana Memo + updates Reputation
          ↓
7. Live Dashboard shows real-time P&L, equity curve, feature cards

docs.title: Agent-facing contract regression
docs.text: The deterministic runner checks the tool and execution behavior an agent sees. It calls the real MCP dispatcher, fee-aware constraint checker, and sequential spread executor with frozen inputs, mocked venue HTTP responses, and a scripted trader. It does not call an LLM or place live orders. Socket connections are blocked, and no credentials or exchange accounts are needed.

docs.title: Run from a fresh checkout
docs.text:
Use Python 3.10 or later, from the repository root:

python -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/python -m pip install -e .
.venv/bin/python scripts/check_agent_contracts.py

On Windows, use .venv\Scripts\python.exe instead of .venv/bin/python. Installing dependencies needs network access; executing the runner does not. The runner prints JSON to stdout and exits with status 0 when all cases pass, or 1 if any case fails. To save the report:

.venv/bin/python scripts/check_agent_contracts.py --output /tmp/oracle3-contracts.json

The output records Oracle3/MCP and installed dependency versions, source Git revision and dirty status, a source-content fingerprint, fixed case IDs, pass/fail status, and structured evidence. It has no timestamps or random inputs. Repeated runs with the same code and dependencies produce the same JSON. MCP error wording can differ between SDK versions; compare case IDs and behavioral outcomes across versions rather than expecting byte-identical reports.

docs.title: Frozen cases
docs.text:
Case ID Required behavior mcp.reject_negative_quantity Reject a negative contract count and identify the invalid input. mcp.reject_unknown_relation Reject a relation outside the supported schema. mcp.preserve_venue_error Surface a mocked HTTP 404 as a tool error, not a successful empty result. mcp.fees_remove_thin_edge Distinguish a positive gross price gap from a negative edge after fees. relation.conditional_not_verified Explicitly mark the relation and execution as unverified. execution.exact_full_fill Recognize two terminal fills for their full requested quantities. execution.partial_fill_is_incomplete Reject basket success for a terminal partial fill; report the exact remaining exposure. execution.failed_unwind_keeps_exposure Report an unsuccessful reverse order and retained exposure without claiming a hedge. execution.open_remainder_requires_reconciliation Preserve known residuals and skip automatic unwind while an order may still fill.

The relation case deliberately supplies an incomplete outcome set while labeling it event_sum. The price checker cannot discover an omitted outcome from those quotes. The conditional price calculation can be positive even though the basket pays zero if that omitted outcome occurs. Passing this case means the output exposes its assumptions and assessment flags; it does not mean Oracle3 has verified the settlement relationship.

Execution evidence includes requested legs, observed order results, reverse-order attempts, known residual quantities, and uncertainty requiring reconciliation. These are simulated exchange responses. The executor is sequential and does not provide atomic transactions across venues.

docs.title: What the report establishes
docs.text:
This is a small regression suite for tool and environment behavior, not a research benchmark. It does not measure an agent's reasoning, skill triggering, relationship detection, live fill probability, or trading performance. It does not establish profitability, production readiness, or superiority over another project. Separate LLM or skill evaluations need labeled tasks, fixed model and prompt configurations, baselines, and an explicit evaluation protocol.

The cases live in scripts/check_agent_contracts.py. Add a stable case ID when a new externally visible failure is fixed, and update this table with the behavior it protects. The runner's own tests check repeatability, failure reporting, nonzero failure exit status, and the network block.

.venv/bin/python -m pip install pytest pytest-asyncio
.venv/bin/python -m pytest -o addopts='' tests/test_agent_contract_harness.py

docs.title: Spread execution
docs.text:
all_filled now requires nonempty requested legs and exact terminal fill confirmations. An empty result is not a completed spread. hedged is true only when reverse fills neutralize the attempt's known position changes and there is no unresolved execution state. An attempted unwind alone does not establish this.

Consume to_payload() for requested orders, observed fills, unwind_results, signed residual_exposures, execution_uncertain, and requires_reconciliation. Residuals describe this attempt, not total account positions. An empty residual list with uncertain execution still requires venue reconciliation: an outstanding order could fill later. The executor does not cancel orders or infer finality after an adapter exception. Uncertain execution skips automatic unwind; confirmed terminal partial fills may attempt recovery. This in-memory helper does not provide durable recovery after process loss or coroutine cancellation; those interruptions require independent reconciliation.

docs.title: Event-sum strategies
docs.text:
EventSumArbStrategy does not trade until configured with a complete partition:

{
  "event_id": "verified-event",
  "outcome_market_ids": ["market-a", "market-b"],
  "yes_token_ids": {"market-a": "yes-token-a", "market-b": "yes-token-b"},
  "outcomes_are_exhaustive": true,
  "outcomes_are_mutually_exclusive": true
}

These are caller assertions that require rule review, not a semantic proof. All declared markets and the relevant quote sizes must be available. An unexpected market invalidates the declaration. trade_size means equal shares per leg. Fees default to oracle3.fees.PolymarketSchedule; supply current per-market market_fee_rates where known. The optional legacy fee_rate is an explicit flat per-share override, not a venue fee schedule. This strategy stops after an incomplete leg but does not automatically neutralize earlier fills; its orders remain sequential.

docs.title: Model comparisons
docs.text: FairValueEstimator.estimate(..., reference_probability=...) accepts an independent probability forecast available at the decision time. Its mispricing_signal is now a signed price residual in dollars per contract: observed price minus the model-adjusted forecast. Without a reference it is exactly zero and excluded from opportunity ranking; this means no independent comparison was made, not that the market has been proved correctly priced. The decomposition-only fair_value and risk_premium remain available.

docs.title: Constraint checks
docs.text: check_constraint and check_constraint_live reject nonfinite quantities, out-of-range quotes, blank market identities, and duplicate contracts. Equal IDs on different venues are distinct. The additive assessment object exposes that rules and execution have not been verified; a positive conditional edge must not be interpreted as an unconditional trade instruction.

docs.title: Runtime and installed-package checks
docs.text: See runtime integrity and migration for accounting semantics, order journaling, retry behavior, strategy ownership and recovery limits. CI additionally builds and installs a wheel outside the checkout and checks a real MCP stdio session on supported SDK 1.x and 2.x versions.

docs.title: Use Oracle3 from an AI agent
docs.text: Use Oracle3 to find Kalshi or Polymarket contracts, inspect quotes and fees, and calculate a basket's price gap under a stated relationship between its outcomes. Public market reads need no exchange account or API key. The MCP server also supports a local paper ledger; no MCP tool places real orders.

docs.title: Choose the code you run
docs.text:
pip install oracle3 and uvx --from oracle3 oracle3-mcp run the published package. The main checkout can contain changes that are not released yet. The assessment fields, paper retry handling and regression runner below describe main; do not infer their availability from a package version badge alone.

For current main, clone and install a checkout:

git clone --branch main https://github.com/YichengYang-Ethan/oracle3-prediction-market-agent.git
cd oracle3-prediction-market-agent
python -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/python -m pip install -e .
git rev-parse HEAD

Record that commit when sharing a result. On Windows, use .venv\Scripts\python.exe for the Python commands. Installation needs network access; the first calculation below does not.

In a client that accepts an mcpServers configuration, replace the example path with the absolute path to this checkout's executable:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "oracle3": {
      "command": "/absolute/path/oracle3-prediction-market-agent/.venv/bin/oracle3-mcp",
      "args": []
    }
  }
}

For Windows, use the absolute path to .venv\Scripts\oracle3-mcp.exe, escaping backslashes in JSON. For Claude Code the equivalent is:

claude mcp add oracle3 -- /absolute/path/oracle3-prediction-market-agent/.venv/bin/oracle3-mcp

Choose one configuration for oracle3 and reload the connection. The client starts the stdio server; it is not an interactive shell. See the MCP reference for published-package configuration and other transports.

docs.title: First call: a deterministic fee check
docs.text:
After the client discovers the tools, call check_constraint with these arguments. A and B are fictional labels; this is a calculation example, not an observed trading opportunity.

{
  "relation": "implication",
  "quotes": [
    {"market_id": "A", "venue": "kalshi", "yes_bid": 0.60, "kalshi_multiplier": 1},
    {"market_id": "B", "venue": "kalshi", "yes_ask": 0.55, "kalshi_multiplier": 1}
  ],
  "contracts": 100,
  "maker": false
}

The supplied premise is A implies B. The checker derives the NO ask on A as 1 - 0.60 and prices 100 NO contracts on A plus 100 YES contracts on B. On current main, this is a subset of the returned data:

{
  "violated": true,
  "profitable_after_fees": true,
  "best": {
    "description": "NO on A + YES on B",
    "cost": 95.0,
    "fees": 3.4125,
    "gross_edge": 5.0,
    "net_edge": 1.5875
  },
  "assessment": {
    "relation_verified": false,
    "execution_verified": false,
    "conditional_on_relation": true
  }
}

Amounts are dollars for the requested basket size. violated reports a positive gross gap; profitable_after_fees applies the calculated fees. Neither verifies the event relationship, liquidity for the requested size, or simultaneous fills. Read assumptions, missing_quotes, and every leg. If no basket can be priced, best is null. Invalid inputs and venue failures are tool errors, not successful empty results.

docs.title: Match the task to a tool
docs.text:
Task Tool Inputs that matter Find candidates search_markets venue, query, limit; Kalshi also supports series_ticker Inspect metadata and available rules get_market venue, market_id Read prices and fee terms get_quote venue, market_id Inspect displayed depth get_orderbook venue, market_id, depth Calculate on supplied quotes check_constraint relation, ordered quotes, contracts, maker Calculate with live quotes check_constraint_live relation, ordered markets, contracts, maker Inspect supported labels / saved relations list_relation_types, list_relations Saved relations remain claims to review Simulate a buy / inspect local holdings paper_order, paper_portfolio See the local paper section below

MCP venues are kalshi and polymarket. Kalshi's market_id is its ticker; Polymarket's is its Gamma market ID, not a CLOB token ID. On Polymarket, the tool's yes and no mean the first and second outcome tokens; inspect the outcome labels, especially for head-to-head markets.

trading_fee is a pure single-fill calculation. fair_value returns a model-implied probability under a chosen Wang-transform parameter; it does not independently verify an event probability.

docs.title: Research a live pair
docs.text:
1. Call search_markets separately with {"venue":"kalshi","query":"fed","limit":10} and {"venue":"polymarket","query":"fed decision","limit":10}.
  2. Pass returned IDs to get_market, for example {"venue":"kalshi","market_id":"<returned ticker>"}. Compare outcomes, deadlines, and settlement sources. Kalshi responses include rules_primary and rules_secondary; Polymarket responses include rules and resolution_source when supplied by the venue. If fields are missing or ambiguous, check the venue's contract rules before assuming equivalence.
  3. State the proposed relation and supporting rules. event_sum requires a complete, mutually exclusive outcome set; a shared event ID is insufficient. If rules are missing or incompatible, report the unresolved question.
  4. Inspect each get_orderbook for the requested size. For a proposed same-event pair, call check_constraint_live with this object, replacing both placeholders:
{
  "relation": "same_event",
  "markets": [
    {"venue": "kalshi", "market_id": "<returned Kalshi ticker>"},
    {"venue": "polymarket", "market_id": "<returned Gamma market ID>"}
  ],
  "contracts": 10,
  "maker": false
}

Report the declared relation, gross edge, fee on each leg, net edge, displayed depth, and assumptions. Live quotes are snapshots; check_constraint_live does not certify depth or fills. Public reads require network access, not trading credentials. Review the returned fee terms instead of assuming every market uses the same defaults.

docs.title: Local paper side effects
docs.text:
For paper execution, paper_order accepts arguments such as {"venue":"kalshi","market_id":"<returned ticker>","side":"yes","contracts":1,"limit_price":0.55,"request_id":"experiment-01-leg-1"}. It walks a live-book snapshot and writes ~/.oracle3/mcp_paper_ledger.json, or the path in ORACLE3_MCP_LEDGER. Inspect status and, for a fill, requested, filled, fees and levels; a partial fill is not a completed basket. Each leg is a separate simulation call. Quantities must be finite and positive, and the limit finite and strictly between 0 and 1; invalid order inputs fail before HTTP.

Use an optional nonblank request_id for retries. Once a result is saved, the same key with identical venue, market, side, quantity and limit returns it without another fill or venue request; changing the intent is an error. Unfilled and rejected results are remembered too. Use a new key for a deliberate new attempt and a distinct key for each leg. Without a key, every call is a new order.

paper_portfolio takes {} and reads that ledger. It supports buys, carries holdings at cost, and does not track resolution or P&L. This ledger is separate from the CLI paper engine. paper_reset with {"confirm":true} erases paper holdings, fills and retry history; without confirmation it changes nothing. Reads, orders and resets lock across cooperating processes on a local filesystem and use atomic writes. Sharing a ledger path shares one account; use separate paths for experiments that need separate state.

Valid older ledgers load automatically. Invalid JSON, nonfinite values or inconsistent accounting produce an error and preserve the file, including when reset is requested. Preserve a copy and restore a valid backup, or point ORACLE3_MCP_LEDGER at a fresh path and restart the server. Do not edit the ledger or delete its .lock sidecar while servers are using it.

docs.title: Agent skills
docs.text:
MCP supplies tools; skills supply workflow instructions. Installing Python packages or configuring MCP does not install these skills into a client.

Skill source Workflow pm-constraint-arbitrage Review a relation and its fee-adjusted basket through MCP pm-data-discovery Discover markets and collect research samples pm-quant-strategy-authoring Author a parameterized quantitative strategy pm-agent-strategy-authoring Author an LLM- or tool-driven strategy pm-paper-trade-ops Run and inspect the CLI paper engine pm-live-trade-ops Operate the separate live CLI when explicitly requested

Inside this checkout, Claude Code loads the .claude/skills/ mirror; Cursor also supports that directory. For Codex, copy the selected skill folder from skills/ into your project's .agents/skills/. Outside this checkout, copy the folder to the client-supported project or user skills directory, preserving its SKILL.md and supporting files. Check for an existing same-named skill before copying; keep the MCP connection configured separately. CLI-based skills also need the checkout's .venv/bin on the agent's executable search path (Windows: .venv\Scripts).

Start with pm-constraint-arbitrage, confirm it appears in the client's skill list, and ask the client to use it for the first-call example. Current discovery instructions: Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex.

docs.title: Replay the tool contracts
docs.text:
From the installed main checkout:

.venv/bin/python scripts/check_agent_contracts.py --output agent-contracts.json

This offline runner exercises frozen MCP errors, conditional checks, and sequential execution failures against mocks. It emits structured evidence and fails on regressions. It evaluates tool and execution behavior, not LLM reasoning, skill effectiveness, or strategy returns. See agent contract regression for cases and migration notes.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Oracle3 applies two risk layers before recording a live Solana trade. The local layer evaluates portfolio limits before a transaction is requested, while the on-chain layer simulates the signed transaction with Solana JSON-RPC immediately before submission. The simulation verifies whether the transaction would execute without a runtime error; it does not replace the local position, exposure, drawdown, or loss controls.

docs.title: Component diagram
docs.text:
graph LR
    Strategy --> TradingEngine
    TradingEngine --> SolanaTrader
    SolanaTrader --> RiskManager
    RiskManager -. wrapped by .-> OnChainRiskManager
    SolanaTrader --> OnChainRiskManager
    OnChainRiskManager --> SolanaRPC[Solana RPC]
    SolanaTrader --> JitoSubmitter
    JitoSubmitter --> SolanaRPC

TradingEngine provides the event loop and binds the strategy to the trader. When the strategy places an order, SolanaTrader coordinates both risk layers: it calls RiskManager.check_trade() before requesting a transaction, then calls OnChainRiskManager.simulate_transaction() after signing it and before either Jito or standard RPC submission.

docs.title: Local risk checks
docs.text:
OnChainRiskManager wraps StandardRiskManager and delegates its first decision to StandardRiskManager.check_trade() (oracle3/risk/onchain_risk_manager.py:86). The local checks run in sequence and reject the trade as soon as one fails:

Guard Behavior Source Maximum single trade Rejects when quantity * price exceeds max_single_trade_size. oracle3/risk/risk_manager.py:89 Position limit Rejects a buy that would exceed max_position_size for the ticker; sells reduce the position and pass this guard. oracle3/risk/risk_manager.py:94 Total exposure Excludes cash from current exposure and rejects a buy that would exceed max_total_exposure. oracle3/risk/risk_manager.py:115 Drawdown Tracks peak portfolio value and rejects when current drawdown reaches the configured maximum. oracle3/risk/risk_manager.py:134 Daily loss When configured, rejects after portfolio loss exceeds daily_loss_limit. oracle3/risk/risk_manager.py:156 Open positions Rejects a new buy when max_positions is reached, while allowing sells and additions to existing positions. oracle3/risk/risk_manager.py:169

SolanaTrader.place_order() also performs order-shape, short-selling, and available-cash checks before the risk manager is called (oracle3/trader/solana_trader.py:343).

docs.title: On-chain pre-flight
docs.text:
After the DFlow Trade API returns a serialized transaction, SolanaTrader deserializes and signs it. If its risk manager is an OnChainRiskManager, the trader sends the signed bytes to simulate_transaction() before submission (oracle3/trader/solana_trader.py:171).

The method base64-encodes the signed transaction and sends this JSON-RPC request (oracle3/risk/onchain_risk_manager.py:110):

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 1,
  "method": "simulateTransaction",
  "params": [
    "<base64 signed transaction>",
    {
      "encoding": "base64",
      "commitment": "confirmed",
      "replaceRecentBlockhash": true
    }
  ]
}

Oracle3 reads result.value.err and result.value.logs from the response. A non-null err rejects the transaction and prevents submission. A null err permits submission, and the log count is written only at debug level. The current implementation does not independently enforce compute-unit limits, inspect account writes, or calculate slippage from the simulation response; those concerns must be handled by transaction construction, local risk rules, or upstream APIs.

docs.title: MEV protection
docs.text:
When Jito support is enabled, SolanaTrader passes the validated signed transaction to JitoSubmitter.submit_with_jito() (oracle3/trader/jito_submitter.py:70). The submitter creates a two-transaction bundle containing the trade and a SOL tip, then sends it to the Jito Block Engine. If Jito rejects the bundle or the request fails, the submitter falls back to Solana sendTransaction with RPC pre-flight enabled (skipPreflight: false) (oracle3/trader/jito_submitter.py:200).

After either Jito or standard RPC returns a signature, SolanaTrader polls getSignatureStatuses until the transaction is confirmed, finalized, failed, or times out (oracle3/trader/solana_trader.py:211). Positions are updated only after confirmation succeeds.

docs.title: Failure modes
docs.text: Failure Current behavior Simulation RPC timeout, transport error, or malformed response simulate_transaction() catches the exception and fails open, allowing submission to continue. The later submission and confirmation steps can still reject the trade. BlockhashNotFound or another simulation error The error appears in result.value.err, so simulation returns False and SolanaTrader blocks submission. replaceRecentBlockhash: true reduces stale-blockhash failures during simulation but does not guarantee later inclusion. Simulation succeeds but submission RPC rejects Standard submission raises an error; Jito submission falls back to standard RPC. The order returns an unknown failure and no position is recorded. Submission returns a signature but execution fails getSignatureStatuses reports a non-null err; confirmation returns False and no position is recorded. Confirmation does not arrive within 30 seconds Confirmation returns False; the order is treated as failed even though final network outcome may require separate reconciliation.

docs.title: oracle3-extras
docs.text: oracle3-extras is Oracle3's companion package, the way pymc-extras relates to PyMC. It holds integrations with wallets, data providers and venues, and features that need real-world use before they belong in Oracle3.

docs.title: What it adds
docs.text: Feature Module What it does Kairos cross-venue pairs oracle3_extras.market.kairos Reads Kairos's public matched-market catalog, lines up the outcomes of every pair across Kalshi, Polymarket, Predict.fun and Hyperliquid, and saves the Kalshi–Polymarket ones as Oracle3 same_event or complement relations Live no-arbitrage scans oracle3_extras.arbitrage Runs check_constraint over thousands of relations with batched quotes, then sizes the survivors against the order books MetaMask Agent Wallet oracle3_extras.trader.metamask A Trader that executes on Polymarket through Agent Wallet, so Oracle3 never holds a private key (testnet by default)

docs.title: Install and try it
docs.text:
pip install git+https://github.com/YichengYang-Ethan/oracle3-extras.git
oracle3-extras kairos pairs --rejected   # aligned pairs, and why the others were left out
oracle3-extras kairos sync               # save them where list_relations reads
oracle3-extras kairos scan               # read-only: cross-venue edges after fees

After kairos sync, the MCP server sees the pairs: list_relations lists them, and each relation's markets can be passed straight to check_constraint_live.

docs.title: How it relates to Oracle3
docs.text:
• Same namespaces. oracle3_extras.market, oracle3_extras.arbitrage and oracle3_extras.trader mirror oracle3.market, oracle3.arbitrage and oracle3.trader, and build on their classes (MarketRelation, check_constraint, Trader).
  • One-way dependency. oracle3-extras depends on one Oracle3 minor series; Oracle3 does not depend on it.
  • Graduation. A feature that people use, that is tested to Oracle3's standard and that needs no partner account moves into Oracle3 at the same path, and the extras version warns for one release before it is removed.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: New integrations and experimental features start in oracle3-extras. Its contributing guide lists what every integration needs: tests without network access, safe defaults, a transparent attribution section and a named maintainer.

docs.title: MCP server
docs.text: Oracle3 ships a Model Context Protocol server that gives AI agents read access to Kalshi and Polymarket, the venues' fee schedules, fee-aware no-arbitrage checks, and a local paper-trading ledger. No tool can place a real order.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
For a released package, use the dedicated server entry point:

pip install oracle3
oracle3-mcp                              # stdio, for desktop and IDE clients

Run this as a client-managed subprocess; stdio waits for MCP protocol input. oracle3 mcp is an equivalent CLI entry point; it also accepts --transport streamable-http for HTTP. Use a virtual environment for pip installs and configure the absolute path to its server executable.

This page describes current main. The explicit assessment fields, paper retry handling and execution contracts were added after release 1.2.2. For those behaviors, follow the source installation in the agent quickstart. The quickstart also provides an offline first call with exact arguments and expected output.

docs.title: Configure a client
docs.text:
Claude Code:

claude mcp add oracle3 -- uvx --from oracle3 oracle3-mcp

Claude Desktop, Cursor and other clients that read an mcpServers block:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "oracle3": { "command": "uvx", "args": ["--from", "oracle3", "oracle3-mcp"] }
  }
}

The server is listed in the MCP Registry as io.github.YichengYang-Ethan/oracle3.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
Tool Arguments Returns Side effects search_markets venue, query, limit, series_ticker Open markets with best prices read-only get_market venue, market_id Prices, volume, timing and venue-provided rules; Polymarket resolution source read-only get_orderbook venue, market_id, depth YES and NO bids and asks, best first read-only get_quote venue, market_id Best bid and ask on both sides, the market's fee schedule read-only check_constraint_live relation, markets, contracts, maker Every basket's cost, fees and edge, with live quotes read-only check_constraint relation, quotes, contracts, maker The same, on quotes you supply none trading_fee venue, price, contracts, maker, schedule parameters Fee for one fill none fair_value market_price, lam Probability implied under the Wang transform none list_relation_types Supported relations and their bounds none list_relations market_id, spread_type, status Relations saved locally, for example by oracle3-extras kairos sync reads ~/.oracle3/relations.json paper_order venue, market_id, side, contracts, limit_price, optional request_id Fill against the live book, with fees; original result on retry writes the paper ledger paper_portfolio Cash, positions, fill count reads the paper ledger paper_reset confirm Fresh ledger erases the paper ledger

Prices are dollars per contract. On Kalshi, market_id is the ticker; on Polymarket it is the Gamma market id, "yes" is the first outcome token and "no" the second. The paper ledger lives at ~/.oracle3/mcp_paper_ledger.json unless ORACLE3_MCP_LEDGER points elsewhere.

Polymarket market details return rules from the upstream description and resolution_source from resolutionSource. Obtain missing or ambiguous rules from the venue's market page and verify the outcome mapping before assuming a relationship. The MCP paper ledger is separate from the trading engine's paper state. Use your client's tools/list response for the installed server's complete JSON input schemas; older releases may differ.

docs.title: Local paper orders and retries
docs.text:
Call paper_order with a returned market ID and a distinct retry key for each intended order, for example:

{
  "venue": "kalshi",
  "market_id": "<returned ticker>",
  "side": "yes",
  "contracts": 1,
  "limit_price": 0.55,
  "request_id": "experiment-01-leg-1"
}

contracts must be finite and positive; limit_price must be finite and strictly between 0 and 1. Invalid order inputs fail before venue requests. Once a result is saved, the same nonblank request_id with identical venue, market, side, quantity and limit returns it without another fill or venue request. Changing that intent is an error. Unfilled and rejected results are also remembered: use a new key for a deliberate new attempt. Without request_id, each call is a new order. paper_reset with {"confirm":true} clears positions, fills and retry history; without confirmation it changes nothing.

Ledger reads, orders and resets use an interprocess lock and atomic file replacement. This assumes cooperating processes using this implementation on a local filesystem; the same path shares one paper account. Use separate paths for separate experiments. Positions remain at cost: this ledger does not track resolution or P&L, and each basket leg is a separate simulation.

Valid older JSON ledgers load without a manual migration. Malformed JSON, nonfinite values or inconsistent accounting cause an error and leave the file intact; even paper_reset refuses to overwrite it. Preserve a copy, then restore a valid backup or configure a fresh ORACLE3_MCP_LEDGER path and restart the server. Do not edit the ledger or remove its .lock sidecar while servers are using it.

docs.title: Relations
Fees
docs.text:
Each quote carries the fee schedule the venue reports for that market:

  • Kalshi: taker round_up(0.07 · M · C · P · (1 − P)), maker round_up(0.0175 · M · C · P · (1 − P)) only on series with maker fees; M is the series fee_multiplier.
  • Polymarket: taker C · rate · p · (1 − p) with the market's feeSchedule.rate; makers pay nothing.

The derivation of what these fees mean for arbitrage is in Do prediction-market arbitrage edges survive fees?.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Ask an agent: "Is the Fed-hold contract on Kalshi priced consistently with the same contract on Polymarket after fees?" A typical tool sequence:

  1. search_markets(venue="kalshi", series_ticker="KXFEDDECISION") and search_markets(venue="polymarket", query="fed decision")
  2. get_market on the two candidates; compare their settlement rules and outcome mappings, consulting venue pages when returned fields are missing or ambiguous
  3. check_constraint_live(relation="same_event", markets=[{"venue": "kalshi", "market_id": "<ticker>"}, {"venue": "polymarket", "market_id": "<id>"}])

The result lists both baskets (YES on Kalshi + NO on Polymarket, and the reverse) with the fee on each leg and the edge left after fees.

docs.title: Oracle3: from U Lab research to reusable agent infrastructure
docs.text:
Project development and maintenance: Yicheng Yang

Oracle3 builds on prediction-market research and software from U Lab at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. It brings market data, structured tools, reusable agent workflows, and an execution environment together in an open-source Python project.

GitHub repository · Connect an agent · MCP tool reference

docs.title: Work at U Lab
docs.text:
Yicheng Yang worked directly with Haofei Yu on Coinjure, contributing to the lab's prediction-market software. He also co-developed the original U Lab Oracle3 codebase with Haofei. This work provided the foundation for his continued development of Oracle3.

Coinjure established an agent-driven workflow spanning market discovery, strategy development, and trading operations. Oracle3 extends that foundation with additional interfaces, reusable workflows, and infrastructure for building and evaluating agents.

docs.title: Yicheng Yang's subsequent development
docs.text:
Yicheng develops and maintains the Oracle3 extensions in this repository. The work focuses on making the underlying system easier to connect to, build on, and evaluate:

Area What Oracle3 provides MCP integration Thirteen tools for Kalshi and Polymarket market discovery, market details, order books, relationship checks, and local paper trading Reusable agent Skills Six documented workflows covering data discovery, constraint checks, strategy authoring, and paper/live operations Market reasoning tools Shared fee calculations and five relationship checks that return structured baskets, costs, and assumptions Execution infrastructure Python strategy interfaces, paper/live adapters, risk controls, and inspectable execution state; MCP paper operations use a separate local ledger Evaluation infrastructure A reproducible software harness, automated tests, and installed-package checks across MCP SDK versions Open-source access A packaged CLI and MCP server, client setup guides, examples, documentation, and a machine-readable project index

These layers support a practical workflow: an agent can discover contracts, inspect their rules and order books, calculate a fee-aware comparison, and record a simulated position. Developers can use the Python interfaces to build their own strategies and experiments. Real-order execution belongs to the separate trading engine; the MCP interface provides market reads, calculations, and paper operations.

docs.title: Why this is useful for agent research
docs.text:
Prediction markets provide a concrete environment for sequential decisions: agents observe changing information, use tools, manage state, and evaluate the consequences of their actions. Oracle3 makes these components available through explicit interfaces that can be reused across agent implementations.

The broader development direction is a shared environment for studying how agents use tools and follow workflows. Three questions motivate further work:

  • Tool design: How do structured inputs, outputs, and state information affect task completion and the number of tool calls?
  • Workflow guidance: What does a reusable Skill add beyond a tool schema and a task prompt?
  • Evaluation harnesses: How can the same tasks and environment be used to compare agent implementations reproducibly?

A planned model-level evaluation would hold the environment and task budgets fixed while comparing tool interfaces and Skill configurations. It would measure completion from the resulting state, alongside tool use and token cost. The current harness validates software behavior; model-level experiments are the next research step.

docs.title: Explore the project
docs.text:
• Agent quickstart: connect an MCP client and run a worked task.
  • MCP reference: inspect the tools, arguments, and returned data.
  • Source code: explore the strategy, market, and execution modules.
  • Automated validation: inspect the software test and package-compatibility results.

docs.title: Origin and contribution boundaries
docs.text:
We acknowledge the foundational work of the Coinjure team at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign—Haofei Yu, Yicheng Yang, Yuxiang Liu, and Prof. Jiaxuan You—on which Oracle3 builds.

Oracle3 retains the original U Lab and Coinjure attribution and MIT license notices in NOTICE. Yicheng Yang maintains the subsequent extensions described above. Software citation information is available in CITATION.cff.

docs.title: Runtime integrity and migration
docs.text: These changes are on the repository's main branch. They are not a claim of live profitability or a replacement for venue-account reconciliation. A published package only includes them after its release contains this commit.

docs.title: Accounting
docs.text:
The engine's performance ledger uses cash plus marked inventory. Entry cash outflow is not a trading loss. Entry and exit fees are allocated to FIFO closing lots; total_trades counts those matched closing lots and total_fills counts fills. One sale can close several lots. This count is not a round-trip count.

Reports expose realized_pnl, unrealized_pnl, total_fees, cash, inventory_value, valuation_complete, and missing_marks. A missing quote carries the previous mark or opening cost, while marking valuation incomplete. A genuine zero bid is a zero mark. A quote's presence does not certify freshness, executable depth, or a liquidation price for the entire position. Completeness describes the current snapshot; drawdown uses observed/carried marks and cannot reconstruct unobserved price changes between observations.

sharpe_ratio=0 is a compatibility placeholder when sharpe_available=false; it is not an estimate. Irregular fill observations are not annualized as daily returns. Research selection excludes unavailable metrics; selecting on marked PnL is exploratory and does not establish predictive performance.

The analyzer supports explicit seed_position, mark_to_market, and binary settle events. It does not automatically fetch or authenticate venue settlement outcomes. Engine restart restores a paired position/accounting checkpoint from runtime.json. Legacy positions without that checkpoint establish a new session cost baseline, not reconstructed historical performance. Inconsistent or corrupt recovery data raises an error. The checkpoint is single-writer and is not a transaction spanning a remote venue and the local intent journal.

docs.title: Orders and interruptions
docs.text:
Kalshi and Polymarket adapters retain client and venue order identifiers. Live CLI sessions use a durable SQLite intent journal scoped to public account identity. Direct Python callers must supply journal_path and a suitable journal_namespace; the constructor default is an in-memory journal. Run one live writer per account/namespace: SQLite reserves identical keys atomically, but it is not a distributed account/inventory lock.

Reuse a client_order_id only for the same intent. A reserved ID is never resubmitted, including after an ambiguous submission failure. A duplicate is an explicit result, not a second order. Confirmed incremental fills enter accounting once. Pending orders, contradictory reports, missing costs/fees, and unknown outcomes require reconciliation and block further order submission. The engine polls pending orders while the feed is idle and suspends strategy execution while reconciliation or checkpoint persistence remains unresolved.

Kalshi accounting uses reported fill costs and fees. Polymarket matching is not settlement finality: associated trades must confirm the actual quantities and prices. Fee-bearing executions without verified net cash/share amounts remain unresolved. This conservative limitation can prevent unattended continuation on fee-bearing markets; it does not imply those markets are unsupported by the venue itself.

A restart with previously applied fills or unresolved intents remains blocked until account inventory and journal state are independently reconciled. There is currently no automatic account-wide reconciliation/resume command. Do not delete the journal or clear a guard to retry an uncertain order. An order ID that cannot be recovered requires account-level investigation. A saved cash balance alone cannot certify positions. The implementation does not cancel outstanding orders automatically or guarantee exactly-once execution across a remote venue.

The existing portfolio risk breach and emergency kill switch stop all order submission, including sales. They are stop controls, not liquidation routines.

docs.title: Multi-leg strategies
docs.text:
Implication, exclusivity, conditional, and structural strategies use shared fee schedules and explicit basket execution outcomes. They track quantities filled by their own strategy instance and never close unrelated account inventory. Failed exits retain known residual exposure. An uncertain order stops subsequent legs and automatic unwind; a terminal, confirmed partial execution can attempt recovery of known fills. Recovery itself can fail.

execution_state() exposes the basket state, owned quantities, and most recent execution evidence. Ownership is local to the strategy instance; it is not a durable allocation ledger across restarts. Restarting with open strategy baskets requires independent position attribution before resuming. Sequential orders are not atomic transactions.

Configuration changes:

  • fee_rate=None uses venue schedules through oracle3.fees; an explicitly supplied legacy rate is a flat per-contract override. market_fee_terms supplies known market-specific schedules. Missing rates in a present fee schedule are errors; they never mean zero fees.
  • min_edge is measured after entry fees using executable basket quotes. Future exit fees and slippage are additional costs.
  • Opaque Polymarket token IDs require explicit yes_token_ids mappings.
  • Conditional baskets use the appropriate bound's hedge direction and weight. Structural baskets use the fitted slope's sign and magnitude. These are assumption-dependent expectation/convergence trades, not guaranteed-payoff arbitrages. Estimated relationships can fail.

Other contributed strategies and the Solana live adapter have not acquired all of these lifecycle guarantees. Extending a venue or strategy requires separate contract tests.

docs.title: Agent queues and installed packages
docs.text:
AgentStrategy.queue_trade stages an intent; it is not an execution receipt. execute_pending_trades drains that queue once and returns observed outcomes. A caller with custom execution must explicitly drain via take_pending_trades. Rebuilding tools with an unhandled queue raises instead of silently discarding it. The related-market example prioritizes queued tool requests over a duplicate final JSON action and uses one execution path.

CI builds a wheel, installs it outside the checkout, and verifies actual stdio MCP initialization, tool listing, a deterministic tool call, and shutdown with supported MCP 1.x and 2.x versions. The contract harness records source/dependency provenance. These are software regressions, not evaluations of LLM reasoning or Skill effectiveness. See the agent contract harness and MCP ledger retry contract.

docs.title: Do prediction-market arbitrage edges survive fees?
docs.text:
Oracle3 research note. Fee schedules retrieved 2026-09-28. Reproduce every number with python scripts/fee_frontier.py.

Related contracts are tied together by probability. If A implies B, P(A) cannot exceed P(B); if an event has n exclusive outcomes, their probabilities sum to one. When quoted prices break one of these bounds, a basket of contracts that pays a known amount in every state can be bought for less than that amount. The question is how large the gap has to be before the basket is worth buying, once every leg pays the venue's fee.

This note answers that from the published fee schedules alone. It uses no market data, so it says nothing about how often such gaps appear. It says how large they must be.

docs.title: The fee on one leg
docs.text:
Both venues charge taker fees proportional to p(1 − p), where p is the price paid for the contract:

Venue Taker fee Maker fee Source Kalshi round_up(0.07 · M · C · P · (1 − P)) round_up(0.0175 · M · C · P · (1 − P)), only on series with maker fees Kalshi Fee Schedule, "Last updated and effective: July 7, 2026" Polymarket C · rate · p · (1 − p), with a per-market rate none; makers are never charged docs.polymarket.com, "Trading fees"

On Kalshi, M is the series multiplier. It is 1 for most series and 0 for a few fee-free ones; the API reports it as fee_multiplier. Polymarket documents default rates of 0.07 for crypto, 0.05 for sports, economics, culture and weather, 0.04 for finance, politics, mentions and tech, and 0 for geopolitics. Each market reports its own rate in the Gamma API's feeSchedule. Among the 100 highest-volume active markets on 2026-09-28, the rates were 0.05 (41 markets), 0.04 (14), 0.07 (13), 0.03 (12) and 0 (7), and 13 markets had fees disabled.

The fee peaks at a price of 0.50, where a Kalshi taker leg costs 1.75¢ per contract, and falls to zero at the extremes. A Kalshi taker leg and a Polymarket crypto leg cost the same.

docs.title: Two-leg baskets
docs.text:
An implication, exclusivity, complement or cross-venue basket has two legs. The break-even violation per contract is the sum of the two legs' fees:

Leg 1 Leg 2 both legs at 0.1 both legs at 0.3 both legs at 0.5 Kalshi taker (M=1) Kalshi taker (M=1) 1.26¢ 2.94¢ 3.50¢ Kalshi taker (M=1) Polymarket politics/finance (0.04) 0.99¢ 2.31¢ 2.75¢ Kalshi taker (M=1) Polymarket sports/economics (0.05) 1.08¢ 2.52¢ 3.00¢ Polymarket politics/finance (0.04) Polymarket politics/finance (0.04) 0.72¢ 1.68¢ 2.00¢ Polymarket crypto (0.07) Polymarket crypto (0.07) 1.26¢ 2.94¢ 3.50¢ Polymarket geopolitics (0) Polymarket geopolitics (0) 0.00¢ 0.00¢ 0.00¢

A one-cent mispricing between two mid-priced contracts is not tradable with taker orders on either venue. At mid prices the violation has to exceed 2 to 3.5 cents per contract before any edge is left.

docs.title: Buying every outcome of an event
docs.text:
For an event with n exclusive outcomes priced p_1, …, p_n that sum to about one, buying every outcome costs a total fee per contract of

k · Σ p_i (1 − p_i) = k · (1 − Σ p_i²)

where k is the taker coefficient. With equal prices this is k · (1 − 1/n), which grows with the number of outcomes:

Outcomes (equal prices) Kalshi taker (M=1) Polymarket politics/finance (0.04) Polymarket sports/economics (0.05) 2 3.50¢ 2.00¢ 2.50¢ 3 4.67¢ 2.67¢ 3.33¢ 5 5.60¢ 3.20¢ 4.00¢ 10 6.30¢ 3.60¢ 4.50¢ 20 6.65¢ 3.80¢ 4.75¢

Many-outcome events are where the sum of quoted prices most often drifts away from one, and they are also where the fee hurdle is highest. On Kalshi it approaches 7 cents.

docs.title: Rounding on small orders
docs.text:
Kalshi's schedule rounds each fee up so that fee plus position cost lands on a centicent ($0.0001). Its illustrative table rounds to the cent. The difference only matters for small orders:

Contracts at $0.50 Centicent rounding Cent rounding (schedule table) 1 $0.0175 $0.02 2 $0.0350 $0.04 5 $0.0875 $0.09 10 $0.1750 $0.18 100 $1.7500 $1.75

oracle3.fees uses centicent rounding by default and increment=CENT reproduces the table.

docs.title: Where edge can still exist
docs.text:
• Fee-free markets. Polymarket markets with a zero rate and Kalshi series with M = 0.
  • Maker legs. Polymarket makers pay nothing, and most Kalshi series charge no maker fee. A resting order may never fill, though, and a basket with one filled leg and one resting leg is a directional position until the second leg fills.
  • Legs at extreme prices. The fee falls toward zero as a leg's price approaches 0 or 1.
  • Size. Fees scale linearly with size, so size does not change the break-even violation. Depth does: the displayed size at the best price limits how much of a violation can be captured.

docs.title: What this note does not show
docs.text: It does not measure how often violations above these thresholds occur, how long they last, or how deep the book is when they do. It assumes every leg fills at the quoted price and that the relation between the contracts is specified correctly, including their resolution rules. Settlement differences between venues can turn an apparent same-event arbitrage into two different bets.

docs.title: Checking a live pair
docs.text:
The MCP server applies these schedules to live quotes. For two markets you believe describe the same event:

check_constraint_live(relation="same_event",
                      markets=[{"venue": "kalshi", "market_id": "<ticker>"},
                               {"venue": "polymarket", "market_id": "<gamma id>"}])

The result reports the cheapest basket, its gross edge, the fee on each leg under that market's own schedule, and the edge left after fees.
